_readme: Knowledge base for e-waste plastic items. Each key is a Stage 1 class name. 'typical_plastic' is the most likely polymer based on item type and era — it is a probabilistic guess, NOT a confirmed identification. Polymer type is only confirmed when a resin code is read by the OCR stage. All hazard and regulation notes should be verified against current local guidelines before use in a public-facing system. Fields marked VERIFY/CITE need a real source before submission.

keyboard.recyclable_note: Recyclable at authorised e-waste facilities; not in general municipal plastic bins due to mixed materials and potential BFR content.
keyboard.bfr_note: Keyboards manufactured before ~2010 are more likely to contain brominated flame retardants (BFRs) in the ABS casing. Post-2010 units may comply with RoHS. VERIFY/CITE: RoHS Directive 2011/65/EU and its India equivalent.
hazards: BFR-treated ABS releases toxic fumes (HBr, dioxins) if burned — do not incinerate
May contain small amounts of lead solder on internal PCB
Keycap dyes may contain heavy metal pigments in older units
handling_rules: Wear nitrile gloves when disassembling
Do not break or shred casings — fine ABS dust is an inhalation hazard
Remove the PCB before sending the plastic shell for recycling
Store in a cool, dry place away from heat sources
reuse_options: Disassemble and sell keycaps individually (mechanical keyboard community)
Donate working units to schools or NGOs
Strip and sell the internal PCB and metal backplate separately
ABS plastic shell: shred and pelletise at a plastics recycler for injection moulding feedstock
keyboard.regulation_note: Under India's E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022, keyboards are listed as IT and telecom equipment. Producers have Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) obligations. Consumers should hand over to an authorised PRO (Producer Responsibility Organisation) or collection point. VERIFY/CITE: Schedule I of E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022.
keyboard.source: VERIFY/CITE — add Kaggle/Roboflow dataset reference and regulatory source here

mouse.recyclable_note: Recyclable at authorised e-waste facilities after removal of PCB and scroll-wheel assembly.
mouse.bfr_note: Similar risk profile to keyboards. Older units more likely to contain BFRs. VERIFY/CITE.
hazards: BFR-treated ABS — do not burn
Internal PCB contains lead solder and potentially cadmium
Optical sensor lens may contain trace rare earth elements
handling_rules: Wear gloves during disassembly
Separate PCB, cable, and plastic shell before recycling
Do not dispose in general waste
reuse_options: Donate working units
Harvest the PCB and scroll encoder for electronics hobbyists
ABS shell suitable for plastics recycling after cleaning
mouse.regulation_note: Same as keyboard — IT and telecom equipment under E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022. Hand over to authorised recycler or PRO. VERIFY/CITE: Schedule I.

charger_casing.recyclable_note: PC and PC/ABS are technically recyclable but require specialised facilities. Mixed with internal transformer and electronics — disassembly needed first.
charger_casing.bfr_note: Charger casings are near heat-generating components and frequently treated with BFRs for fire safety compliance. This is especially true for older or uncertified chargers. VERIFY/CITE: IEC 62368-1 fire safety requirements.
hazards: High BFR content likely — do not burn or shred without respiratory protection
Internal capacitors may hold residual charge even when unplugged
Transformers in older chargers may contain PCB-based insulating oil (very old units) — VERIFY/CITE
Nickel and lead in solder joints
handling_rules: Discharge capacitors before disassembly (short the output terminals through a resistor)
Wear gloves and a dust mask when cutting or breaking the casing
Never burn — toxic halogenated gases
Send to authorised e-waste recycler as a complete unit if not disassembling
reuse_options: Working chargers: donate or resell
Casing plastic: send to BFR-capable plastics recycler — do NOT mix with general plastics
Internal copper transformer windings have scrap value
PCB: send to precious metal recovery
charger_casing.regulation_note: Chargers fall under IT and telecom equipment in E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022. Given the BFR risk, prefer authorised hazardous e-waste handlers. VERIFY/CITE.

printer_casing.recyclable_note: Large volume of plastic but complex disassembly. Most recyclers will take the whole unit.
printer_casing.bfr_note: Printer casings — especially laser printers — are strong BFR candidates. Laser printers generate ozone and fine toner particles during operation, and casings are treated accordingly. VERIFY/CITE.
hazards: HIPS with BFR — do not burn
Toner cartridges contain carbon black (potentially carcinogenic at high dust levels) — handle carefully
Laser printer fuser units reach high temperatures — burn risk during disassembly
Selenium drum in laser printers: selenium is toxic — do not crush or incinerate
handling_rules: Remove toner cartridges first and recycle separately through manufacturer take-back schemes
Wear an N95 mask when handling toner-contaminated parts
Allow laser printer to cool completely before disassembly
Wear gloves — toner is a fine powder that penetrates skin
reuse_options: Working units: donate to schools, NGOs, or resell
Toner cartridges: many manufacturers (HP, Canon, Epson) run free take-back programmes
Casing plastic (HIPS/ABS): send to authorised BFR plastics recycler
Metal frame and rollers: scrap metal recycler
printer_casing.regulation_note: Printers are listed under IT and telecom equipment in E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022. Toner cartridges are separately regulated as consumables. Hand over to PRO or authorised collection centre. VERIFY/CITE.

tv_panel.recyclable_note: High BFR probability makes standard plastic recycling unsuitable. Requires specialised e-waste facility.
tv_panel.bfr_note: CRT TV back panels are among the highest BFR-risk items in consumer e-waste. HIPS with decaBDE or TBBPA flame retardant was standard practice until the mid-2000s. LCD/LED TV panels from post-2010 may comply with RoHS but verify by checking the resin code and manufacturer documentation. VERIFY/CITE: Stockholm Convention on POPs (decaBDE listing).
hazards: Very high BFR content in older CRT casings — never burn, never melt without specialist equipment
CRT glass contains ~2–3 kg of lead per unit — separate and send to lead recycler
CRT vacuum implosion risk — never drop or strike a CRT
LCD backlights (CCFL in pre-LED units) contain mercury — handle as hazardous waste
Capacitors in PSU retain charge
handling_rules: Treat old CRT TV casings as hazardous material — double-bag if broken
Do not burn, grind, or shred
Wear gloves, safety glasses, and N95 mask during disassembly
Keep away from children
Transport upright — CRTs are fragile
reuse_options: Working TVs: donate or resell
CRT glass: specialist CRT glass recyclers (lead recovery)
HIPS/ABS back panel: BFR-capable plastics recycler only
Copper yoke and degaussing coil: scrap copper value
LCD panel glass: flat glass recycler
tv_panel.regulation_note: Televisions are listed as consumer electrical and electronic equipment under E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022. CRT TVs are particularly regulated due to lead glass. Must be handed to an authorised recycler — do not dispose in general waste. VERIFY/CITE: Schedule I, Category 3.

remote.recyclable_note: ABS remote casings are generally recyclable at e-waste facilities. Low BFR risk in modern units.
remote.bfr_note: Modern remotes typically use ABS without heavy BFR treatment. Older units (pre-2000) may have some BFR content. VERIFY/CITE.
hazards: Batteries inside are the main hazard — always remove before disposal
Button cell batteries contain mercury (older) or lithium — handle as hazardous
Rubber keypad membrane may contain carbon black
handling_rules: Remove all batteries before disposal — recycle batteries separately
Do not crush or incinerate
ABS casing can go to general e-waste collection
reuse_options: Working remotes: donate with the parent device
Universal remote: reprogramme and reuse
IR LED and receiver: harvest for electronics projects
ABS casing: standard ABS recycling stream
remote.regulation_note: Remotes as standalone items fall under miscellaneous consumer electronics. Batteries removed from remotes must be disposed of under Batteries Management and Handling Rules. Hand over to authorised collection point. VERIFY/CITE.

other_plastic.recyclable_note: Cannot determine recyclability without identifying the polymer. Use Stage 2 OCR to read the resin code.
other_plastic.bfr_note: Any plastic part that was close to heat-generating components (power supplies, motors, transformers) is a BFR candidate regardless of item type.
hazards: Unknown polymer — treat as potentially hazardous until resin code is confirmed
If near heat sources in original device, assume BFR presence
handling_rules: Do not burn
Wear gloves
Try to read the resin code (Step 2 in the app) before deciding on disposal route
If no code found, send to authorised e-waste recycler
reuse_options: Identify polymer via resin code, then follow the specific route for that polymer
If unidentifiable, send to authorised e-waste facility — do not mix into general plastics
other_plastic.regulation_note: All e-waste plastic must be handled under E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 regardless of whether the specific polymer is known. Hand over to authorised PRO or recycler. VERIFY/CITE.

unknown.recyclable_note: This item was not recognised as a known e-waste plastic item. If it is e-waste, try a clearer photo. If it is not e-waste, this app does not apply.
handling_rules: Retake the photo with better lighting and a plain background.

ABS.notes: Most common e-waste plastic. Hard, opaque, impact-resistant. Softens at ~105°C. Can contain BFRs. Do not mix with general household plastics.

PC/ABS.notes: Common in charger casings, laptop shells. Higher heat resistance than pure ABS. BFR risk similar to ABS.

PC.notes: Transparent or translucent. Used in LED diffusers, optical discs. Generally lower BFR risk than ABS in e-waste context.

HIPS.notes: Common in older TV and monitor casings. High BFR risk in these applications. Not the same recycling stream as food-grade PS.

PP.notes: Used in battery casings, cable clips, some appliance parts. Generally low BFR risk. Recyclable code 5.

PVC.notes: Common in cable insulation. Contains chlorine — burning produces HCl and dioxins. Never incinerate. Contains plasticisers (phthalates) that are endocrine disruptors. Avoid skin contact with old PVC cables.

PE.notes: Used in cable sheathing, bags, packaging. Low hazard. Recyclable codes 2 (HDPE) and 4 (LDPE).
